summary: The developer machine has the key run-time pieces and DocumentDB MCP data-plane tools needed to build the FastAPI cohort-snapshots sample against the live cluster. Most of the model's cold answers about the service were outdated or conflated older Cosmos DB 'databaseAccounts' / RU-based APIs with the newer vCore DocumentDB offering (mongoClusters). The build can start, but agents should apply the concrete corrections below (resource type = Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters, az documentdb / az cosmosdb mongocluster CLI commands, vCore billing model, Microsoft Entra ID support, integrated $search and vector indexes) and add a couple of developer conveniences (DocumentDB Agent Kit and a local DocumentDB Docker image or mongosh) if desired.
summary_points: All required runtime tools for a Python FastAPI sample are present (python, pip, Docker) and the DocumentDB data-plane MCP server is available; you can start building and verifying against the live cluster.

Many cold answers conflated older Cosmos DB (databaseAccounts / RU model) or other products with the current Azure DocumentDB mongoClusters (vCore) offering — builders must use mongoClusters docs and az documentdb/ mongocluster commands.

Key factual corrections: resource type is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters; capacity is vCore compute + storage (not RUs); Microsoft Entra ID (OIDC/MONGODB-OIDC) is supported for data-plane access; integrated $search and vector indexes (IVF/HNSW/DiskANN) exist.
Accelerators that would speed the work are missing (DocumentDB Agent Kit skill and locally runnable DocumentDB image or mongosh). These are not blockers but will save time.
The sample database sample_customer_360_15 exists but contains no collections — the builder must include an idempotent seed script and create the expected indexes before verifying snapshots.

tools.name: python
tools.needed_for: Run the FastAPI app, create virtualenv, run seed scripts and tests (pip install, uvicorn).
tools.impact_if_missing: Cannot run the sample or install Python dependencies locally.
tools.workaround: Not practical; install Python. Use a container with Python if local install is impossible.

references.title: Quickstart: Use Azure DocumentDB with MongoDB driver for Python

tools.name: pip
tools.needed_for: Install Python dependencies (pymongo, fastapi, uvicorn, python-dotenv, apscheduler).
tools.detail: pip available via Python virtual environment
tools.impact_if_missing: Cannot install or run the sample from source.
tools.workaround: Use a container that has dependencies preinstalled or include a prebuilt wheel bundle.

tools.name: documentdb
tools.needed_for: Data-plane inspection and verification: run aggregations, create collections and indexes, explain plans, insert sample data and examine collections on the live cluster.
tools.detail: DocumentDB MCP server present and returns 18 tools (aggregate, explain, list_indexes, insert_documents, list_databases, ...). Connection profile 'default' required for calls.
tools.impact_if_missing: Builder couldn't programmatically inspect or verify collections/indexes and couldn't run aggregation tests against the live cluster.
tools.workaround: Use mongosh (CLI) or the Azure portal to inspect resources if mongosh is available; otherwise rely on driver-level checks. For automation, install the documentdb MCP toolkit.

tools.name: learn (Microsoft Learn docs MCP)
tools.needed_for: Authoritative documentation search & fetch to ground service facts (resource types, CLI, connection examples, feature docs).
tools.impact_if_missing: Agent can't quickly verify up-to-date doc facts and code samples.
tools.workaround: Use external web search or local copies of docs.

tools.name: az
tools.needed_for: Inspect control-plane resources, read cluster properties, and (if needed) enable features or list firewall rules via az documentdb / az cosmosdb groups.
tools.detail: Azure CLI 2.89.1 installed and signed in (az login). cosmosdb-preview / documentdb extensions may be present in extensions list.
tools.impact_if_missing: Harder to read or change cluster properties and to enable preview features from CLI.
tools.workaround: Use the Azure portal to view and update cluster settings.

tools.name: docker
tools.needed_for: Run a local DocumentDB gateway for integration tests and dev parity (the sample-run environment prefers the live cluster but local image speeds iteration).
tools.impact_if_missing: No local DocumentDB instance for offline testing; must run tests against remote cluster.
tools.workaround: Run tests against the live cluster or use mock frameworks; pull the local DocumentDB container image if desired.

tools.name: mongosh
tools.needed_for: Manual connectivity checks and ad-hoc verification (`mongosh` is a common manual tool to inspect collections, run explain plans, and test connection strings).
tools.impact_if_missing: Manual interactive checks will be slightly more awkward; the MCP documentdb server provides scripted data-plane tools, but many developers expect mongosh.
tools.workaround: Use the documentdb MCP server's aggregate/find/explain tools or the Visual Studio Code DocumentDB extension, or install mongosh.

tools.name: git
tools.needed_for: Source control for the sample code repository.
tools.impact_if_missing: Harder to clone or manage source; developer can still copy files manually.
tools.workaround: Use zip downloads or other SCM.

tools.name: documentdb-driver (skill)
tools.needed_for: Driver best-practices (singleton MongoClient, connection pooling) to implement the FastAPI app safely and efficiently.
tools.detail: Installed skill documentdb-driver present in skill folder
tools.impact_if_missing: Risk of implementing client connections incorrectly (creating per-request clients, connection exhaustion).
tools.workaround: Follow generic PyMongo documentation; prefer one MongoClient per process.

tools.name: documentdb-connection (skill)
tools.needed_for: Connection tuning (pool sizes, timeouts) for production-like workloads and serverless patterns.
tools.impact_if_missing: Harder to tune connection pooling for FastAPI and async frameworks safely.
tools.workaround: Use conservative defaults from driver docs and the documentdb-driver skill recommendations.

tools.name: documentdb-indexing (skill)
tools.needed_for: Index selection guidance for the cohort aggregation and retention queries.
tools.impact_if_missing: Risk of running heavy aggregations without appropriate indexes leading to COLLSCAN and slow pipelines.
tools.workaround: Follow general indexing guidance from MongoDB and verify with explain(), or run documentdb_explain_operation in the MCP server.

tools.name: documentdb-natural-language-querying (skill)
tools.needed_for: Generate example aggregation pipelines (using $bucket, $facet) adapted to the actual collection schema to implement cohort computations.
tools.detail: Installed skill documentdb-natural-language-querying present; requires documentdb MCP server to sample documents.
tools.impact_if_missing: Harder to author correct aggregation pipelines quickly.
tools.workaround: Manually author pipelines using MongoDB aggregation docs and test via documentdb_aggregate and explain tools.

tools.name: documentdb-local-deployment (skill)
tools.needed_for: Guidance to run DocumentDB locally in Docker for tests and local dev (gateway image on 10260, TLS notes).
tools.impact_if_missing: Harder to set up local DocumentDB dev image and follow recommended TLS options.
tools.workaround: Follow the public Docker quickstart page and the skill's docs; docker is already installed so the image can be pulled.

tools.name: azure_sign_in (credential)
tools.needed_for: Read-only control-plane checks via az (if the sample needs to optionally enable features or view resource settings).
tools.detail: az login present and signed-in to subscription 'Visual Studio Enterprise Subscription'
tools.impact_if_missing: Cannot query or change Azure control-plane settings used for feature enablement (for example enabling FullTextSearch preview via resource patch).
tools.workaround: Use portal access or request an account with az login rights.

accelerators_missed: DocumentDB Agent Kit (agent skills bundle) — would speed rule-of-thumb decisions, concrete sample scaffolding and templates; install with: npx skills add Azure/documentdb-agent-kit

Local DocumentDB Docker image (DocumentDB local) — a container image to run a local gateway for integration tests; pull and run: docker pull ghcr.io/documentdb/documentdb/documentdb-local:latest && docker run -d -p 10260:10260 --name documentdb-local ghcr.io/documentdb/documentdb/documentdb-local:latest --username admin --password secret

mongosh (developer convenience) — interactive shell for ad-hoc queries and explain plans (install from MongoDB downloads), useful though not strictly required because the documentdb MCP server offers programmatic equivalents

confusions.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Resource type: databaseAccounts (full type: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts). Example ARM/Bicep resource type: "Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts@2021-04-15".
confusions.grounded_answer: The current resource type used to deploy the vCore managed Mongo clusters is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (examples in the ARM/Bicep / template docs for mongoClusters).

grounding_links.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters (templates listing)
Azure CLI: az documentdb mongocluster create

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Older Cosmos DB documentation and the historically common resource type Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (Cosmos 'databaseAccounts') are similar names; the vCore offering uses a new resource type (mongoClusters).

confusion_sources.title: Azure Cosmos DB (databaseAccounts) ARM resource docs (example pages still present)

confusions.build_risk: Using Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts in deployment templates or CLI calls will either create the wrong resource (Cosmos DB account) or fail to produce a vCore mongo cluster; the code that expects mongoClusters resources (connection strings, cluster-level controls) will not work.
improvements: Update quickstarts and sample scaffolds to use Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters for vCore clusters instead of the older databaseAccounts examples.
Add a deprecation/clarification note on the 'databaseAccounts' docs explaining that vCore mongoClusters use the mongoClusters resource type.

confusions.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the core CLI group az cosmosdb. Example: az cosmosdb create --name my-account --resource-group my-rg --kind MongoDB ... The cosmosdb commands are in the core az CLI (no separate extension required).
confusions.grounded_answer: The supported CLI commands for vCore clusters are exposed as az documentdb mongocluster (and az cosmosdb mongocluster aliases in some docs). Use az documentdb mongocluster create / update / show / firewall-rule etc. (learn docs show az documentdb mongocluster create).

grounding_links.title: az documentdb mongocluster create

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Older Cosmos CLI guidance used az cosmosdb for databaseAccounts; the vCore mongoClusters commands are surfaced under az documentdb / az cosmosdb mongocluster and are newer.

confusion_sources.title: az cosmosdb mongocluster create (alternate doc page showing cosmosdb alias)

confusions.build_risk: Using az cosmosdb create with databaseAccounts parameters will create a different resource (a Cosmos account) and not the vCore mongo cluster; CLI scripts and automation would fail to create or manage the intended resource.
improvements: In CLI quickstarts and generator templates, call out the correct command group (az documentdb mongocluster) and provide examples.
Add an inline note in the az cosmosdb docs to point users to az documentdb mongocluster for the vCore offering.

confusions.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
confusions.grounded_answer: For vCore clusters use the Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters ARM/Bicep resource (learn templates list mongoClusters); Terraform examples use the mongoClusters resource via ARM/Bicep/AzAPI (see mongoClusters template docs).

grounding_links.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters (ARM/Bicep/Terraform templates pages)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Older Cosmos DB examples and the azurerm_cosmosdb_account Terraform resource target databaseAccounts (the RU model); vCore clusters are a different resource surface (mongoClusters).

confusion_sources.title: azurerm_cosmosdb_account Terraform docs (older Cosmos DB examples)

confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong resource type in IaC will provision the wrong service (a Cosmos DB account) or fail to deploy the vCore cluster; generated templates would not be usable to create a DocumentDB mongoClusters cluster.
improvements: Update Bicep/Terraform quickstarts to show Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters for vCore clusters and add a migration note for older databaseAccounts examples.
Add an example AzAPI/Terraform snippet that uses the mongoClusters reference so agents can produce correct IaC.

confusions.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
confusions.cold_answer: Typical CosmosDB (Mongo API) connection string: mongodb://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retrywrites=false&maxIdleTimeMS=120000&appName=@<account>@. SRV not generally provided.
confusions.grounded_answer: For Azure DocumentDB vCore clusters you obtain cluster connection strings from the portal / API; production cluster strings commonly use mongodb+srv://<client-or-username>@<cluster-name>.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com/?tls=true&authMechanism=SCRAM-SHA-256 (and SRV is supported for some connection flows and for Microsoft Entra OIDC flows documented). The portal 'Connection strings' blade is authoritative — use the exact returned connection string and follow the provider docs for TLS and authMechanism options.

grounding_links.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using MongoDB Shell
Get cluster connection strings and private endpoint notes

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Older Cosmos DB (RU model) and earlier Mongo-compatible account endpoints used the .mongo.cosmos.azure.com host and the 10255 TLS port; vCore clusters and the DocumentDB gateway expose connection string formats and SRV forms and recommend using the portal-provided string.

confusion_sources.title: Cosmos DB Mongo API legacy connection examples (still present in some docs)

confusions.build_risk: Using an incorrect connection string format or wrong port can make the driver fail to connect or use incorrect authMechanism options; the builder must take the portal-provided string or the cluster's listConnectionStrings output.
improvements: Document a canonical example connection string for mongoClusters in the 'how to connect' quickstart and highlight use of mongodb+srv and MONGODB-OIDC where applicable.
Add a short note in the quickstart that users must copy the exact connection string from the portal/cluster and not assume a fixed host suffix/port.

confusions.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
confusions.cold_answer: Cosmos DB (including the MongoDB API) is billed in Request Units (RUs) ... there is also a newer vCore-based preview SKU but the common model is RUs.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB (vCore managed Mongo clusters) is billed by compute tier (vCores) and storage — you choose cluster tier (M10, M20, M30, M40...) and storage per shard. The RU model applies to Cosmos DB request-unit based accounts; vCore DocumentDB uses vCore+storage pricing.

grounding_links.title: Azure DocumentDB pricing explained (compute tiers and vCores)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The Azure Cosmos DB 'RU' billing model applies to the RU-based Cosmos accounts; the vCore (M#) tiers for DocumentDB are a different billing model and share overlapping naming/brand history.

confusion_sources.title: Azure Cosmos DB RU model docs (older guidance)

confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes RUs, they might attempt to use RU-specific APIs or provision throughput in IaC and fail, or choose an inappropriate scaling approach (wrong API calls and wrong cost estimates).
improvements: Clarify the pricing page and quickstarts to explicitly say: 'DocumentDB (vCore) uses compute tiers (M10/M20/M30...) + storage; Cosmos DB RU model is different.'
Add an explicit 'choose your model' decision box in migration and quickstart pages so agents pick the right provisioning and billing model.

confusions.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
confusions.cold_answer: For the MongoDB API you normally authenticate with Cosmos DB-managed Mongo credentials (username/password). Direct Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) authentication is not available to MongoDB drivers in the same way it is for the SQL API.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports native authentication (SCRAM) and Microsoft Entra ID (OIDC/MONGODB-OIDC) for data-plane access when the cluster is configured to allow MicrosoftEntraID. The docs show how to enable authConfig.allowedModes and how to form an OIDC connection string (mongodb+srv://<client-id>@<cluster>.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com/?tls=true&authMechanism=MONGODB-OIDC and the driver-side OIDC callback usage in Python).

grounding_links.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control and Microsoft Entra ID
Python example: connect to the cluster using OIDC callback and DefaultAzureCredential

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Historically the Mongo API on some Cosmos deployments did not support Azure AD data-plane auth; the newer vCore DocumentDB clusters explicitly add Microsoft Entra ID (OIDC) support which some older pages didn't reflect.

confusion_sources.title: Older Cosmos DB Mongo API docs that focused on account keys

confusions.build_risk: If a builder assumes AAD is unavailable they may embed account keys in configs or choose a less secure pattern, or fail to implement OIDC flows recommended for production.
improvements: Add a short example in the 'how to connect' quickstarts showing both SCRAM and Microsoft Entra OIDC connection strings and a Python snippet for DefaultAzureCredential + OIDC callback.
Mark the sections that historically predate OIDC support so agents don't rely on stale pages.

confusions.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
confusions.cold_answer: For the MongoDB API use the standard MongoDB drivers (e.g. Python: pymongo). There is a service-specific SDK (azure-cosmos) for the Cosmos DB SQL API, but for Mongo API you should use the official MongoDB driver for your language.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: use standard MongoDB drivers (pymongo for Python) for DocumentDB's Mongo-compatible clusters; quickstarts show pymongo examples and recommend driver best practices (one MongoClient per process).

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Use Azure DocumentDB with MongoDB driver for Python

confusions.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
confusions.cold_answer: Historically Cosmos DB did not expose native Mongo-style vector index types; if vector-capable option exists it would be provider-specific and use special createIndex with algorithm options (hypothetical).
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports integrated vector indexes and the documentation explicitly describes vector index kinds vector-ivf (IVF), vector-hnsw (HNSW), and vector-diskann (DiskANN) with JSON templates for createIndexes / createSearchIndexes (cosmosSearch options). The docs show example bodies and parameters (dimensions, m, efConstruction, numLists, lBuild, lSearch, similarity metrics).

grounding_links.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB (IVF/HNSW/DiskANN examples)
Quickstart: Use vector search with Python in Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Vector indexes are a newer integrated capability for DocumentDB; if a model has older knowledge about Cosmos DB's lack of integrated vectors or about Atlas-specific vector features it will assume none are available.

confusion_sources.title: Older pages saying Cosmos DB requires Azure Cognitive Search or external vector store

confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes vector indexes are unavailable they might adopt a separate vector DB architecture, adding complexity; conversely, assuming an Atlas-style API will lead to incorrect createIndex calls.
improvements: Add a short 'create vector index' JSON example in the quickstart for Python and highlight supported 'kind' values vector-ivf, vector-hnsw, vector-diskann.
Document the maximum dimension limits and recommended tiers for each index type in a single quick-reference doc.

confusions.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
confusions.cold_answer: Full-text search on Cosmos DB is typically done by integrating with Azure Cognitive Search or using Cosmos DB's integrated search if available; hybrid vector+text usually pairs Azure Cognitive Search with a vector layer.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB offers an integrated full-text search engine (createSearchIndexes and the $search aggregation stage) and supports hybrid retrieval (BM25 keyword + vector) through the cosmosSearch operator and recommended fusion patterns (Reciprocal Rank Fusion). You do not need an external Azure Cognitive Search instance for integrated BM25 text and hybrid queries on DocumentDB.

grounding_links.title: Full-text search in Azure DocumentDB (createSearchIndexes and $search)
Hybrid keyword + vector retrieval (BM25 + vector) guidance

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Some Cosmos DB workflows historically relied on Azure Cognitive Search; DocumentDB's newer integrated search ($search and createSearchIndexes) may be overlooked by models remembering older recommendations.

confusion_sources.title: Azure Cognitive Search + Cosmos integration examples (older guidance)

confusions.build_risk: If the builder insists on provisioning a separate Azure Cognitive Search index they'll add unnecessary infrastructure and complexity; conversely, assuming no integrated search exists would make them implement extra ETL.
improvements: Add an explicit 'full-text search and hybrid retrieval' quickstart for DocumentDB showing BM25 + vector fusion patterns and an example pipeline using $search and cosmosSearch.

confusions.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
confusions.cold_answer: Cosmos DB exposes specific wire versions mapped to server versions (3.2/3.6/4.0/4.2/5.0 and more recently 6.x in some regions). Some features missing: server-side JS (eval), some admin commands, parts of aggregation, change streams historically not supported — use Change Feed.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports modern MongoDB wire protocol versions (documentation lists support for 5.0 through 8.0 in many pages), and provides a compatibility matrix of supported operators and commands. Some administrative/admin commands and server internals are managed by the service; change streams are available but have limitations (resumability caveats across topology changes and other documented limits). Verify feature support against the compatibility docs and run the provided compatibility assessment tool before migration.

grounding_links.title: MongoDB feature compatibility in Azure DocumentDB (compatibility-features)
Change streams in Azure DocumentDB (limitations)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The set of supported wire protocol versions has evolved; statements that change streams were entirely unsupported are outdated — change streams (with caveats) and the service-managed behavior are now documented.

confusion_sources.title: Older compatibility pages describing more limited feature support

confusions.build_risk: Relying on an unsupported operator in production would fail; not checking the documented operator matrix could cause pipeline errors. Use the compatibility assessment tool before migrating complex workloads.
improvements: Merge the compatibility matrix and the change-streams limitations into one 'feature support' page so agents can find change-stream status and per-operator support in one place.

confusions.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the Azure Cosmos DB Emulator; SQL API at https://localhost:8081; Cosmos Mongo emulator endpoint common is 10255. Note emulator parity can lag production.
confusions.grounded_answer: For DocumentDB development there is a local DocumentDB gateway Docker image (ghcr.io/documentdb/documentdb/documentdb-local) that the docs and local-deployment skill recommend; its gateway listens on port 10260 by default (examples show publishing 10260:10260). The Azure Cosmos DB Emulator (8081) is not the right local image for the vCore DocumentDB gateway workflow.

grounding_links.title: DocumentDB local Docker quickstart and gateway on port 10260
Quickstart: Evaluate DocumentDB on Azure Local (port-forward, 10260 examples)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The Cosmos DB emulator and its 8081 endpoint are for the Cosmos SQL emulator and some Cosmos APIs; DocumentDB's local gateway uses a different image and a different port (10260). Models conflated the two emulators.

confusion_sources.title: Azure Cosmos DB emulator docs (SQL emulator, 8081)

confusions.build_risk: Attempting to use the wrong local emulator will either fail to start or be missing features (vector indexes, createSearchIndexes) and cause false negatives during local testing.
improvements: Add a short 'local dev' quickstart that shows the Docker image name and the single-line docker run command using port 10260 so agents don't assume the Cosmos emulator is the right target.

confusions.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
confusions.cold_answer: MongoDB-style change streams were historically not supported for Cosmos DB's Mongo API; use Cosmos DB Change Feed instead.
confusions.grounded_answer: DocumentDB exposes change-stream-like APIs and supports change streams with documented limitations (e.g., topological changes affecting resumability, some event fields unavailable). Also, for some accounts the service provides Change Feed semantics; check the change-streams docs for limitations. Some limitations exist rather than wholesale absence.

grounding_links.title: Change streams in Azure DocumentDB (limitations)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Older product versions and some Cosmos Mongo API accounts lacked change stream semantics; newer DocumentDB clusters support change streams with caveats.

confusion_sources.title: Older guidance recommending Change Feed instead of Mongo change streams

confusions.build_risk: If the app assumes full MongoDB change-stream semantics (global ordering across shards, resumability across topology changes) it may break on resume behavior or miss cases where Azure-managed topology changes require cursor reinitialization.
improvements: Expand the 'change streams' doc to list typical migration pitfalls and a short pattern for resilient resume handling in consumer code.

confusions.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
confusions.cold_answer: Expect a dedicated 'documentdb' MCP server for data-plane inspection; general Azure MCP handles control plane.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: the agent environment contains a 'documentdb' MCP server that provides data-plane tools (aggregate, explain, list_indexes, insert_documents, etc.). The general Azure MCP server exists for control-plane and policy/ARM tasks but not for data-plane explain/aggregate convenience.

grounding_links.title: documentdb (MCP server tools)

confusions.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
confusions.cold_answer: Azure DocumentDB was the original name of Microsoft's proprietary NoSQL service; it was rebranded/expanded into Azure Cosmos DB. The original DocumentDB engine evolved into Cosmos DB, unrelated to open-source DocumentDB.
confusions.grounded_answer: The current Azure DocumentDB (vCore managed MongoDB-compatible service) was previously referred to as the vCore-based Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB and has been renamed to Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility). It is separate from the original 2014-era Azure DocumentDB that became Cosmos DB, and it aligns with the open-source DocumentDB engine. The docs explain these naming relationships and distinctions.

grounding_links.title: What is Azure DocumentDB (naming and history)

confusions.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
confusions.cold_answer: Cosmos DB's Mongo API uses Microsoft's proprietary Cosmos engine; use Mongo drivers but expect behavioral differences.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB (vCore) is implemented on the open-source DocumentDB engine (the DocumentDB project), and some docs state that the engine is built on PostgreSQL internals for storage. The important practical point for builders is: use standard MongoDB drivers (no provider-specific SDK for data plane) but test for a small set of compatibility differences (detailed in the compatibility matrix).

grounding_links.title: What is DocumentDB (in Azure) — engine and implementations
Azure DocumentDB at a glance (engine and compatibility)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Older knowledge that Azure's 'Cosmos' engine powers many APIs led to conflation; the vCore DocumentDB product is explicitly aligned with the open-source DocumentDB engine.

confusion_sources.title: Older pages describing Cosmos engine internals

confusions.build_risk: If a builder assumes Cosmos DB engine internals they may rely on engine-specific admin commands or behaviors not present on the DocumentDB implementation. But application-level Mongo drivers work and are the right integration point.
improvements: Add a short 'engine and compatibility' section to quickstarts: 'DocumentDB engine (open-source) underlies the service — use Mongo drivers and consult the per-operator compatibility table before migrating.'

information_gaps.title: Existing collection/schema in sample_customer_360_15
information_gaps.description: The readiness check must know whether the sample database sample_customer_360_15 already contains collections and which field names are present (customers/events/purchases). I called the documentdb_list_databases tool and the database exists but currently lists no collections; no skill or doc provides the builder's intended collection/field names — the builder must decide a schema and seed script. (Checked: documentdb MCP server via documentdb_list_databases.)

information_gaps.title: Desired sample dataset size and characteristics
information_gaps.description: The prompt doesn't specify how many customers, months of history, or event density are needed for the cohort-retention demonstration. No installed skill prescribes concrete seed sizes; the builder should choose a representative size (for demo ~1k customers over 12 months) and document it. (Looked in prompt and local-deployment skill; no exact size guidance.)

information_gaps.title: Exact endpoint and response shape for cohort API
information_gaps.description: The prompt says 'expose cohort analysis endpoints' but doesn't specify route names, query parameters, or exact response JSON shape. No installed skill decides REST contract; the builder must define and document routes like GET /cohorts and GET /cohorts/{cohort_month} and their JSON schemas.

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Use the Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters resource type (not Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts) and the az documentdb mongocluster CLI commands or the mongoClusters ARM/Bicep templates when referring to vCore clusters.

Treat capacity as vCore compute + storage for DocumentDB vCore clusters (pick an M-tier such as M30) — do not attempt to provision or plan for RU/s. Use the DocumentDB pricing pages to estimate costs.

Obtain the cluster connection string from the portal or from the cluster's listConnectionStrings output and use the standard MongoDB driver (pymongo). For Microsoft Entra ID auth use the MONGODB-OIDC authMechanism and the documented OIDC callback flow (DefaultAzureCredential + OIDC token callback).

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Create search indexes and/or vector indexes using the documented createSearchIndexes/createIndexes patterns (cosmosSearch operator for $search and vector index kinds vector-ivf / vector-hnsw / vector-diskann) rather than assuming an external Cognitive Search dependency.

inventory_recommendations.name: azd
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not required for this Python FastAPI sample; builders can use az CLI or portal to inspect resources. If you plan to use Azure Developer CLI workflows, install azd separately (azd install docs).

inventory_recommendations.name: bicep
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not required for the sample (the run environment says do not provision a new cluster). If you plan to produce Bicep IaC for cluster provisioning, install Bicep (az bicep install) or use the ARM templates shown in the mongoClusters docs.

inventory_recommendations.name: terraform
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not necessary for the sample which reuses an existing cluster, but add the Terraform AzAPI provider if you want example IaC; otherwise document how to use the ARM/Bicep mongoClusters templates.

inventory_recommendations.name: dotnet
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not required for this Python sample. Install only if you plan to produce a .NET sample or use the .NET Azure SDK examples.

inventory_recommendations.name: mongosh
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Install mongosh for convenient ad-hoc connectivity and manual explain-plan checks; otherwise use the documentdb MCP server's documentdb_explain_operation and documentdb_aggregate tools. Install from MongoDB's download pages or via package manager (brew/apt).
